name: Berdazimer gel
lead: Berdazimer gel, sold as Zelsuvmi, is a prescription topical medicine that releases nitric oxide onto the skin to clear molluscum contagiosum, the small, dome-shaped bumps caused by a poxvirus. By clearing these visible lesions, it helps restore smooth, even-looking skin, particularly for children and for adults whose bumps are conspicuous.[2][4]

The FDA authorized Zelsuvmi on January 5, 2024 for people aged one year and older; it is described as the first licensed prescription medication for molluscum that is applied at home.[4] It is applied once daily to lesions for up to 12 weeks and is supplied as two components, a berdazimer gel and a hydrogel, that are combined for use.[4]

Efficacy was examined in vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials, including the 891-participant B-SIMPLE4 study, and in a meta-analysis of four randomized trials with 1,854 patients.[6][2] The most common side effects are local: burning, itching, redness and irritation at the application site.[4]

angle.text: Berdazimer gel is applied daily to molluscum bumps, and in trials a larger share of treated participants reached complete clearance than with vehicle gel. Clearing the bumps removes a visible skin-texture concern, and the trials also tracked scarring.

paras: Berdazimer gel is indicated for molluscum contagiosum in patients aged one year and older.[4] The condition is a common viral skin infection, mostly in children, with lesions that can last months to years and may cause itching, self-consciousness and household spread.[5][12]

Berdazimer sodium is a polymer-based nitric oxide donor. It was developed by Novan Inc., later a Ligand Pharmaceuticals company, using the firm's NITRICIL platform, which stores nitric oxide on large polymers so that it is released once the product is mixed and applied.[16] The prescription product, Zelsuvmi, is supplied as two components, the berdazimer gel and a hydrogel, that are combined immediately before use.[4]

Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus and appears as small, firm, dome-shaped papules, often in groups, that can persist for months to years before clearing on their own. Reviews note that although the condition is benign it can become an aesthetic burden, cause itching or secondary dermatitis, and lead to self-isolation.[2] Before 2024, no medication was FDA-approved for it in the US, and clinicians relied on procedures such as curettage or cryotherapy and on off-label topicals.[17]

Nitric oxide-releasing gels from Novan were first studied in acne under the code names NVN1000 and SB204, with phase 1 to 3 registrations running from 2012 to 2016.[20] The same chemistry, as SB206, was then taken into molluscum. Two phase 3 trials, B-SIMPLE1 and B-SIMPLE2, began in mid-2019, and a third, B-SIMPLE4, began in September 2020.[15][14][13]

The FDA approved berdazimer topical gel, 10.3%, in January 2024 for adults and children aged one year and older, describing it as a first-in-class medication.[16][22] The approval review summarizes the platform and development milestones.[16]

In B-SIMPLE4, adverse events were described as low overall, and the most common were application-site pain and erythema, mostly mild; 4.1% of the berdazimer group stopped treatment because of adverse events, compared with 0.7% of the vehicle group.[17] The meta-analysis of four trials likewise weighed the gain in clearance and reduction in scarring against a higher rate of topical reactions, a point it flags for pediatric use.[2]

The Wikipedia entry lists further application-site reactions such as rash, swelling, erosion, discoloration and blistering, along with fever, vomiting and upper respiratory infections among common effects.[22] The molluscum trials enrolled 1,598 participants at 121 US sites across three studies, which gives the safety database its size.[22]

Zelsuvmi is a prescription-only product in the US. Reports on treatment adherence note that a once-daily, multi-week topical regimen asks a lot of families, and a recent expert consensus guidance document addresses prevention and treatment of molluscum in children.[3][12] A patient-reported substudy of B-SIMPLE4 collected impressions of change from patients and caregivers.[18]

Outside molluscum, nitric oxide-releasing gels have been studied in acne. A phase 2 study reported a significant reduction in non-inflammatory acne lesions against vehicle, but no significant change on the investigator global assessment score.[22]

In the phase 3 B-SIMPLE4 trial, 891 participants aged six months and older with 3 to 70 lesions applied berdazimer 10.3% gel or vehicle gel once daily for 12 weeks; the primary endpoint was complete clearance at week 12.[6][13] A meta-analysis of randomized trials found berdazimer effective for lesion clearance and reported reduced scarring, while noting a higher rate of topical adverse effects that matters particularly for children.[2]

An integrated analysis of three randomized trials, a trial in people with atopic dermatitis, a pharmacokinetic study and a Japanese open-label study have also been published.[8][7][10][11] A systematic review of molluscum treatments describes berdazimer's safety profile as favorable for pediatric patients, and a review on adherence notes that daily topical treatments face adherence challenges.[1][3]

In B-SIMPLE4, run at 55 US clinics, complete clearance at week 12 was 32.4% with berdazimer against 19.7% with vehicle gel.[17] A post hoc analysis of the three phase 3 trials (1,598 patients, 13.1% of whom had atopic dermatitis) reported that the clearance advantage over vehicle also appeared in the atopic dermatitis subgroup, where complete clearance was 35.0% on berdazimer.[7] Patients in that subgroup had more lesions at baseline, averaging 26.4 versus 19.3.[7]

A pooled analysis of four randomized trials with 1,854 patients, 59.6% of them on berdazimer, supported its efficacy for clearing lesions.[2] A Medical Letter review of the drug and a first-approval review in Drugs are also available.[19][16]

The gel generates nitric oxide, which has antiviral properties; the exact mechanism in molluscum is described as unclear but thought to involve inflammation, immune regulation and viral replication.[4] Laboratory work has examined its effect on the molluscum virus in vitro.[9]
Reported effects are mostly at the application site, including burning, itching, redness and irritation.[4]

timeline.event: First nitric oxide gel (NVN1000) phase 1 studies in acne begin.[21]
Phase 3 B-SIMPLE1 and B-SIMPLE2 trials begin.[15][14]
FDA authorizes Zelsuvmi for molluscum in people aged one year and older.[4]

card.summary: A prescription nitric oxide gel that clears molluscum bumps, leaving smoother skin.
card.note: Prescription only; local burning and itching are common.

quick.overview:
Berdazimer gel (Zelsuvmi) is a prescription gel for molluscum contagiosum, the small raised bumps caused by a virus. Applied once daily to the lesions for up to 12 weeks, it releases nitric oxide.

People use it to clear the bumps and return the skin to a smooth, even look. It was FDA authorized in January 2024 for ages one and up.
quick.mechanism: The gel releases nitric oxide on the skin, which has antiviral properties. The exact way it clears molluscum is described as not fully understood.
quick.risks: The most common effects are burning, itching, redness and irritation where it is applied. It is available by prescription in the US.
